title: Al-Bayyinah: the clear proof
hookLine: the People of the Book and others awaited a clear sign (Surah 98)
last: THE EARTH'S REPORT — THE GROUND REMEMBERS.

cards: One day, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ went to a companion named Ubayy ibn Ka'b, a man known for his recitation, and said something strange.
Allah has commanded me to recite to you: those who disbelieve, the opening of Surah al-Bayyinah. Ubayy asked: did He name me? The Prophet said: yes.
And Ubayy wept. It's in Sahih al-Bukhari. A man hears that his own name was spoken by the Lord of the worlds, and he cries.
Of all the surahs, this was the one chosen for that moment.

teach.b: Bayyinah means a clear proof, evidence you can see, something that makes a matter plain. The root is b-y-n, to be distinct, to stand out clearly, the same root as bayan, a clear statement.
The surah opens with people waiting.

Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, a phrase commentators apply to Jews and Christians, and among the polytheists, the surah says, would not let go of their ways until the clear proof came to them.
Then it names that proof: a messenger from Allah, reciting purified pages, containing upright writings. For Muslims, that's the Prophet and the Qur'an he recited.
Then a quiet line: the People of the Book did not divide until after the clear proof had come to them.
Commentators read it as a pattern the Qur'an describes more than once: clarity itself can become the place people disagree. A sign doesn't end argument; sometimes it starts it.
In its closing verses the surah describes two kinds of people and their ends, and speaks of those who believe and do good as the best of creation, well pleased with Allah and He with them.
Tomorrow, the verse in the middle, about what was actually asked of everyone. Today, just the word.
A clear proof makes things plain enough to choose. The Qur'an presents itself that way: not as a riddle, but as bayyinah, something clear. What people do with clarity is another matter.

how: Muslims recite al-Bayyinah in the prayers, and the hadith of the Prophet reciting it to Ubayy ibn Ka'b is often told as a sign of honor for those who learn and recite the Qur'an.

o: a hidden sign only scholars can read
evidence that makes a matter plain to see

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: wept when told he was named

s: the Prophet was commanded to recite this surah to Ubayy
and when Ubayy heard Allah had named him, he wept (Bukhari).
the surah says a clear sign ended all disagreement
it says people divided after the clear proof came.
it means evidence that makes things plain.

games.q: you're Ubayy ibn Ka'b. the Prophet tells you Allah has commanded him to recite this surah to you. what do you ask?
games.why: did He name me? yes. and Ubayy wept (Bukhari).

practice: Bring to mind one short verse you've met here, like by time, or he is one, and say it once, slowly.
Then think of something in your life that is actually clear, that you already know is right, and that you've been putting off anyway. Just let it be plain.

wordCard.voice: Al-Bayyinah. The clear proof, evidence that makes a matter plain; the name of Surah ninety-eight. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the clear proof, from b-y-n, to be distinct and plain.

carryVoice: Your line: clear proof. What's already clear doesn't need a bigger sign. That's day one hundred seventy-eight.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4959 (the Prophet recites it to Ubayy)
